entries.type: reporting verb — statement, formally and deliberately restated
entries.patterns: affirm + that-clause / affirm + noun phrase / affirm + to sb + that-clause / affirm (intransitive, in court)
entries.never: affirm someone that; affirm to do something
entries.meaning: A public, deliberate statement that something is true, usually restating a position already on record. Unlike claim it carries no doubt; unlike confirm it does not require a prior question. Two specialized senses live alongside it: to affirm in court is to make a solemn declaration in place of an oath, and an appellate court affirms a lower court's ruling by letting it stand.
entries.transform: "We remain committed to the treaty," the ambassador said. -> The ambassador affirmed that they remained committed to the treaty.
examples: The board affirmed that no layoffs were planned for the coming year.
She quietly affirmed her belief that the study would hold up.
The witness chose to affirm rather than swear on a Bible.
The appeals court affirmed the conviction in a two-page order.
The ambassador affirmed to reporters that the treaty remained in force.
In his letter he affirmed that the money had been repaid in full.
Nobody at the hearing affirmed that the deadline was still in force.

entries.type: reporting verb — accusation asserted but unproven
entries.patterns: allege + that-clause / allege + noun phrase / be alleged + to-infinitive (passive) / allege + sb + to be (rare, legal)
entries.never: allege to do something (active voice); allege someone something; allege sb that
entries.meaning: The strongest doubt marker in English, and the only one that also carries an accusation. Allege tells the reader two things at once: the statement is unproven, and it charges someone with wrongdoing. That is why journalists reach for it — the accusation is reported without the newspaper adopting it. Use it for wrongdoing only.
entries.transform: "Their auditor destroyed the files," the plaintiff said. -> The plaintiff alleged that their auditor had destroyed the files.
examples: Prosecutors allege that the payments were routed through three shell companies.
The suit alleges a pattern of retaliation going back four years.
She is alleged to have signed the forms without reading them.
None of the alleged victims has been named publicly.
The article carefully alleged nothing it could not document.
He allegedly left the building twenty minutes before the alarm sounded.

entries.type: reporting verb — public statement of news
entries.patterns: announce + that-clause / announce + noun phrase / announce + wh-clause / announce + to sb + that-clause / announce + noun phrase + to sb
entries.never: announce someone something; announce someone that; announce to do
entries.meaning: Making something publicly known, usually for the first time. It presupposes both that the content is true and that it is news, which is why he announced that he was tired sounds like a joke. Plainer and less ceremonial than declare; without any of the grandeur of proclaim.
entries.transform: "We're moving the office to Denver," she told the staff. -> She announced to the staff that they were moving the office to Denver.
examples: The mayor announced that the pool would reopen in June.
They announced the merger an hour before the market opened.
She walked in and announced to nobody in particular that the elevator was broken.
The airline has not yet announced which routes it will cut.
He announced his resignation in a two-sentence email.
Nothing was announced about the second round of funding.

entries.type: reporting verb — a claim advanced with reasons
entries.patterns: argue + that-clause / argue + for/against + noun phrase or -ing / argue + noun phrase / argue + sb + into/out of + -ing / argue + about/over + noun phrase or wh-clause (quarrel sense) / argue + with sb (+ about sth)
entries.never: argue someone that; argue to do something; argue someone to do something (needs into/out of)
entries.meaning: Asserting a position together with the reasons for it. The verb commits the speaker to a supporting case and presupposes that the point is contestable, which makes it the default verb of academic writing. It does not signal doubt the way claim does; it signals contested ground.
entries.transform: "The data don't support that conclusion, and here's why," she said. -> She argued that the data did not support the conclusion.
examples: She argues that the second experiment was never properly controlled.
The defense argued the case for four days.
He argued against expanding the program until the audit was finished.
They argued her into taking the job by promising a relocation budget.
The two of them argued about whether to sell the house.
It could be argued that the whole policy was obsolete by the time it passed.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement made forcefully and without hedging
entries.patterns: assert + that-clause / assert + noun phrase / assert + oneself
entries.never: assert someone that; assert someone something; assert to do something; assert someone to do something
entries.meaning: Stating something as fact, flatly and confidently, usually without offering support. By drawing attention to the confidence rather than the evidence it invites the reader to notice that nothing was proved — a milder doubt marker than claim, but not fully neutral.
entries.transform: "The vote was rigged. Period," he said. -> He asserted that the vote had been rigged.
examples: The report asserts that the software was never tested on live data.
She asserted her right to have a lawyer present.
He asserted, without producing a single document, that the deal had been approved.
The company has asserted control over three of the four subsidiaries.
In meetings she has learned to assert herself early.
Nobody in the room asserted anything they could not back up.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement made to remove someone's doubt
entries.patterns: assure + sb + that-clause / assure + sb + of + noun phrase / assure + sb (alone)
entries.never: assure that with no object (assure is obligatorily ditransitive); assure to sb that; assure sb to do
entries.meaning: Telling someone directly that something is true in order to settle their doubt. Where affirm is oriented toward the record, assure is oriented toward the addressee. Keep it apart from ensure (make certain something happens) and insure (cover with a policy).
entries.transform: "Don't worry — the check went out Monday," she said. -> She assured me that the check had gone out that Monday.
examples: The nurse assured him that the swelling would go down in a day or two.
She assured us of her support before the vote was even scheduled.
I can assure you that nobody here saw the email.
He assured the landlord the rent would clear by Friday.
Rest assured — the file was backed up before the crash.
The contractor assured them repeatedly, and then missed the deadline anyway.

entries.type: reporting verb — formal statement from firsthand knowledge
entries.patterns: attest + that-clause / attest + to + noun phrase or -ing or wh-clause / attest + noun phrase
entries.never: attest to + that-clause (the preposition takes a noun phrase, -ing or wh-clause, never a bare that-clause); attest someone that; attest to do
entries.meaning: Bearing witness — asserting something on the strength of one's own knowledge, in a setting where the statement counts for something. It presupposes the speaker's credibility rather than the truth of the content, which is why an inanimate subject works naturally: the wear on the steps attests to a century of use.
entries.transform: "I saw him sign it," she said. -> She attested that she had seen him sign it.
examples: Two colleagues attested that he had been in the building all morning.
Anyone who has waited in that line can attest to how slow it is.
A notary must attest the signature before the deed is filed.
The scorch marks on the ceiling attest to an earlier fire.
She attested under penalty of perjury that the return was complete.
Nothing in the file attests to a second inspection.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement made positively and on the record
entries.register: formal; legal, literary, rare in speech
entries.patterns: aver + that-clause / aver + noun phrase
entries.never: aver someone that; aver to do something
entries.meaning: Stating something confidently and formally, and in legal pleading, alleging a fact one intends to prove at trial. Outside court filings and self-consciously literary prose it reads as precious or archaic; say said, insisted, or asserted instead.
entries.transform: "I never received the notice," he said. -> He averred that he had never received the notice.
examples: The complaint avers that the contract was signed under duress.
He averred, with a straight face, that he had read every page.
She averred her innocence in the same flat tone all afternoon.
Counsel must aver the facts supporting jurisdiction in the opening paragraphs.
In the memoir he avers that the letter was destroyed by accident.
Nobody in the deposition averred anything about a second meeting.

entries.type: reporting verb — open admission of a belief or allegiance
entries.patterns: avow + that-clause / avow + noun phrase / avow + oneself + noun phrase or adjective
entries.never: avow someone that; avow to do something (that is vow, a different act)
entries.meaning: Declaring openly something one might reasonably be expected to conceal — a belief, a loyalty, a motive. It presupposes candor and a small cost to the speaker. The participle is commoner than the finite verb: an avowed socialist. Its opposite, disavow, denies any connection.
entries.transform: "Yes, I supported the strike, and I still do," she said. -> She avowed that she had supported the strike and still did.
examples: She avowed that her only interest in the case was the principle.
He publicly avowed his support for the boycott a week before the vote.
An avowed skeptic, she read the whole report twice before commenting.
The senator avowed himself satisfied with the compromise.
The company disavowed the memo within hours of its leaking.
Few of them would avow in writing what they said freely in the hallway.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement the writer does not endorse
entries.patterns: claim + that-clause / claim + to-infinitive (same subject only) / claim + noun phrase / claim + sb/sth + to be (formal, rare)
entries.never: claim someone to do something; claim someone that
entries.meaning: The everyday doubt marker of English. Writing he claimed he was home tells the reader in one word that the writer is not vouching for it — said is neutral, pointed out endorses, claimed withholds. Unlike allege it accuses nobody; unlike purport it takes a human subject comfortably. The to-infinitive frame is same-subject only. The formal claim + object + to be frame (the report claimed the signature to be a forgery) is restricted to to be plus a complement and belongs to legal and academic prose; every other object-controlled infinitive is blocked, so a that-clause is always the safe rewrite.
entries.transform: "I paid that invoice in March," he said. -> He claimed that he had paid the invoice that March.
examples: He claims the fence was already down when he got there.
She claimed to have no memory of the conversation.
Two different groups have claimed responsibility for the outage.
The label claims the bottle contains no added sugar.
Nobody has claimed the bag left in the lobby.
They claimed a deduction that the auditor immediately disallowed.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement verifying something already in question
entries.patterns: confirm + that-clause / confirm + noun phrase / confirm + wh-clause / confirm + to sb + that-clause / be confirmed + to-infinitive (passive)
entries.never: confirm someone that; confirm to do
entries.meaning: Stating that something already suggested, rumored, or asked about is in fact true. It is factive — He confirmed that the deal had collapsed commits the writer to the collapse — which is why a newspaper will not use it for a statement it cannot stand behind. It also presupposes a prior question.
entries.transform: "Yes, the flight is canceled," the agent said. -> The agent confirmed that the flight was canceled.
examples: The lab confirmed that the sample was contaminated.
Can you confirm whether the room is still available for Thursday?
He confirmed the appointment by text an hour beforehand.
Two sources have confirmed to the paper that the talks broke down.
The species was later confirmed to be new to science.
Nobody at the agency would confirm who had signed off on the waiver.

entries.type: reporting verb — a claim advanced inside a dispute
entries.patterns: contend + that-clause / contend + with + noun phrase (cope with) / contend + for + noun phrase (compete for)
entries.never: contend someone that; contend to do something; contend + noun phrase in the reporting sense
entries.meaning: Asserting a position in an argument that has another side. Contend presupposes an opponent, which is why it belongs to court reporting and coverage of disputes. It carries a mild doubt tint — the writer is describing one party's position, not the facts — but it is more dignified than claim and accuses nobody.
entries.transform: "The clause never applied to seasonal staff," the union said. -> The union contended that the clause had never applied to seasonal staff.
examples: The defense contends that the search was unlawful from the start.
Critics contend the model breaks down at low temperatures.
He contended that no one had ever explained the fee to him.
Both sides contend that the other walked away from the table.
She has contended for years that the surveys undercount renters.
It has been contended, though never demonstrated, that the two events are linked.

entries.type: reporting verb — formal public statement made with authority
entries.patterns: declare + that-clause / declare + noun phrase / declare + sb/sth + (to be) + complement / declare + oneself + adjective or noun phrase / declare + to sb + that-clause / declare + for/against + noun phrase
entries.never: declare someone that; declare someone something; declare to do
entries.meaning: Stating something formally and with standing, often in a way that makes it so — I declare this meeting adjourned performs an adjournment rather than describing one. Neutral as to truth but loud as to manner, and in ordinary narrative it lends a whiff of theater.
entries.transform: "This election is void," the commission said. -> The commission declared the election void.
examples: The governor declared a state of emergency before the storm made landfall.
He declared that the numbers had been checked twice.
The judge declared the contract unenforceable.
She declared herself satisfied and went home.
You have to declare anything over ten thousand dollars at customs.
Two senators have declared against the bill in its current form.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.patterns: emphasize + that-clause / emphasize + noun phrase / emphasize + wh-clause / emphasize + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: emphasize on (the noun takes on, the verb takes a plain object); emphasize someone that; emphasize to do
entries.meaning: Not a new claim but extra weight on part of one. It is factive: she emphasized that the deadline was firm commits the writer to the deadline being firm. Compared with insist it implies no resistance — the speaker is underlining, not defending. American English spells it -ize; emphasise is British.
entries.transform: "And this is the important part — the deposit is nonrefundable," she said. -> She emphasized that the deposit was nonrefundable.
examples: She emphasized that the results were preliminary.
The coach emphasized footwork all through the first week.
He emphasized how little time was left before the filing date.
The memo emphasized to managers that overtime had to be approved in advance.
Every speaker emphasized the same three numbers.
It cannot be emphasized enough that the backup runs only on weekdays.

entries.type: reporting verb — a settled belief, or a court's binding ruling
entries.patterns: hold + that-clause / hold + sb/sth + (to be) + complement / hold + noun phrase / it is held + that-clause (passive)
entries.never: hold someone that; hold to do something
entries.meaning: Maintaining a position one is settled in rather than arguing toward — a standing belief, a doctrine, or in law the part of a decision that binds later courts. Keep the legal pair straight: a court holds the law and finds the facts. Irregular: hold, held, held.
entries.transform: "In my view, the deadline was never binding," she said. -> She held that the deadline had never been binding.
examples: Most economists hold that the effect is too small to measure.
The Ninth Circuit held that the ordinance violated the First Amendment.
She holds the view that the whole department should be restructured.
It is widely held that the practice began in the 1930s.
He held the study to be worthless and said so in print.
Nobody now holds that the two species are closely related.

entries.type: reporting verb — two acts under one word: a statement held against resistance, and a demand
entries.patterns: insist + that-clause (indicative = claim; bare subjunctive = demand) / insist + on/upon + noun phrase / insist + on/upon + -ing / insist + on/upon + sb + -ing / insist (intransitive)
entries.never: insist someone to do something; insist to do; insist sb that; insist doing (the -ing form always needs on)
entries.meaning: In the claim sense, continuing to assert something against doubt or contradiction — a soft signal that the hearer may not be buying it. In the demand sense, refusing to accept any alternative. The mood of the that-clause decides which act is being reported: American English puts a bare subjunctive in the demand sense (insisted that he be there, insisted that she not be told), and an ordinary tensed clause that backshifts in the claim sense (insisted that he had been there). The subjunctive shows only in the third-person singular and with be, and it has no tense, so reporting leaves it untouched. The same pattern runs after demand, require, request, recommend, propose, urge, ask, and stipulate.
entries.transform: "I insist that he be present," she said. -> She insisted that he be present. / "He was present, I'm telling you," she insisted. -> She insisted that he had been present.
examples: He insisted that the door had been locked when he left.
She insisted that the report be circulated before the meeting, not after.
They insisted on paying for dinner.
The landlord insisted on our signing a two-year lease.
I said no twice, and he insisted anyway.
The union insisted that no one be laid off before the arbitration was finished.
She insists she never received the second notice.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement held to under pressure
entries.patterns: maintain + that-clause / maintain + noun phrase
entries.never: maintain someone that; maintain to do something
entries.meaning: Continuing to assert something in the face of contradiction. Maintain presupposes a challenge already made — the word itself says the position is under attack — so it is a soft doubt marker: the reader infers that somebody credible disagrees. Compare insist, which adds force, and contend, which places the statement inside a formal dispute.
entries.transform: "I've said it before: I was never told," he said. -> He maintained that he had never been told.
examples: He has maintained from the first day that the account was not his.
She maintained her innocence through two trials.
The company maintains that the recall was voluntary.
Both witnesses maintained that the light had been green.
He maintained this position long after his own lawyers gave up on it.
They maintain, against all the evidence, that the map is accurate.

entries.type: reporting verb — formal public commitment
entries.patterns: pledge + to-infinitive / pledge + that-clause / pledge + noun phrase / pledge + sb + noun phrase / pledge + to sb + that-clause / pledge + oneself + to + noun phrase or -ing
entries.never: pledge someone to do something meaning promise them (that frame binds the other person, as in pledged them to secrecy); pledge someone that (the addressee needs to)
entries.meaning: A formal, usually public promise, generally with money, policy, or institutional weight attached. Weaker as a personal oath than vow and less solemn than swear — a government pledges, a person vows. It presupposes an audience: pledges are made where they can be counted.
entries.transform: "We will cut emissions by half," the minister said. -> The minister pledged to cut emissions by half.
examples: The foundation pledged four million dollars over three years.
Both candidates pledged to release ten years of tax returns.
She pledged that no employee would lose health coverage in the transition.
He pledged them his full support and then missed every meeting.
The signatories pledged themselves to a common set of standards.
Donors have pledged more than they have actually paid.

entries.type: reporting verb — a claim put forward as a starting assumption
entries.patterns: posit + that-clause / posit + noun phrase
entries.never: posit someone that; posit to do something; posit about
entries.meaning: Advancing a proposition as a premise, for the sake of argument, without asserting that it is true. It is the lowest-commitment verb in the group — let us posit that the market is efficient concedes nothing about actual markets — which makes it useless for reporting ordinary speech and indispensable in academic writing.
entries.transform: "Suppose, for the moment, that the sample is representative," she said. -> She posited that the sample was representative.
examples: The paper posits that language learning and music share a single mechanism.
Let's posit a reader who has never seen the earlier draft.
She posited an intermediate stage that nobody has yet observed.
Critics say the model posits far more structure than the data support.
He posited that the two outbreaks had a common source, then set out to test it.
Nothing in the theory posits a hard limit on the number of participants.

entries.type: reporting verb — a claim asserted without proof, as a basis for reasoning
entries.patterns: postulate + that-clause / postulate + noun phrase
entries.never: postulate someone that; postulate to do something
entries.meaning: Asserting something as true without evidence in order to build on it. Slightly more committed than posit — a postulate is something you intend to keep, not merely to try out — and much more committed than hypothesize, which invites a test. The final vowel separates verb from noun.
entries.transform: "Assume a fifth planet, and the orbits work," he said. -> He postulated a fifth planet.
examples: Mendel postulated particles of inheritance long before anyone saw a chromosome.
The theory postulates that the two populations were separated for ten thousand years.
She postulated an unobserved intermediate to make the numbers work.
Nothing in the argument requires us to postulate a designer.
He postulated that memory consolidation happens mostly during sleep.
Every one of the postulates was later shown to be unnecessary.

entries.type: reporting verb — loud, public, ceremonial declaration
entries.patterns: proclaim + that-clause / proclaim + noun phrase / proclaim + sb/sth + (to be) + complement / proclaim + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: proclaim someone that; proclaim to do
entries.meaning: Announcing publicly and grandly, with more ceremony than declare and far more than announce. In modern American prose it is very often ironic — he proclaimed the redesign a triumph signals that the writer does not agree. Used straight it belongs to proclamations, coronations, and headlines.
entries.transform: "The revolution has succeeded!" -> They proclaimed that the revolution had succeeded.
examples: The governor proclaimed the first Monday in May a day of remembrance.
She proclaimed that the era of cheap money was over.
He proclaimed himself an expert after reading two articles.
The banner proclaimed a grand reopening that never happened.
Every review proclaimed the album a masterpiece.
Nobody was ready to proclaim victory with a third of the votes uncounted.

entries.type: reporting verb — an open claim about one's own beliefs, feelings, or abilities
entries.patterns: profess + to-infinitive (same subject) / profess + that-clause / profess + noun phrase / profess + oneself + adjective or noun phrase
entries.never: profess someone to do something; profess someone that
entries.meaning: Claiming openly to hold a belief, feel a feeling, or possess a skill — and with the to-infinitive the writer is almost always signaling skepticism. He professes to care about the neighborhood invites the reader to doubt that he does; he says he cares does not. That built-in eyebrow is what separates profess from avow, which presupposes candor.
entries.transform: "I have no idea how the file got there," he said. -> He professed to have no idea how the file had gotten there.
examples: He professes to know nothing about how the money moved.
She professed a lifelong love of opera and then fell asleep in the second act.
Both candidates profess deep concern about the deficit.
The company professes that its supply chain is fully audited.
He professed himself shocked, which fooled nobody.
She professed her innocence in a two-page letter to the editor.

entries.type: reporting verb — an authoritative verdict
entries.patterns: pronounce + sb/sth + complement / pronounce + that-clause / pronounce + on/upon + noun phrase / pronounce + noun phrase
entries.never: pronounce someone that; pronounce to do something
entries.meaning: Delivering a judgment that is official because of who is delivering it. The verdict frame — pronounce + object + complement — is performative: a doctor's I pronounce him dead creates the legal fact. Used of ordinary opinions it is deliberately grand and usually a little arch. The other pronounce, saying a word aloud, is the same word in a different sense.
entries.transform: "The defendant is guilty on both counts." -> The jury pronounced him guilty on both counts.
examples: She was pronounced dead at the scene.
The critic tasted three of them and pronounced the second one best.
The court will pronounce sentence on Thursday morning.
He declined to pronounce on a case still under appeal.
The inspector pronounced the wiring safe and signed the form.
Nobody has pronounced the project finished, but nobody is working on it either.

entries.type: reporting verb — an indignant assertion made against an accusation
entries.patterns: protest + that-clause / protest + noun phrase (American also protest the ruling) / protest + to sb + that-clause / protest + against/at + noun phrase
entries.never: protest someone that; protest to do something; protest someone something
entries.meaning: Asserting something in objection, almost always against a charge, and almost always with the implication that nobody is convinced. "I never touched it," he protested is a sentence in which the reader already suspects he did. American English lets protest take a direct object in the demonstration sense (protested the tuition increase); British English requires protest against.
entries.transform: "But I already sent it — twice!" she said. -> She protested that she had already sent it twice.
examples: He protested that the charge had never appeared on any statement he received.
She protested her innocence loudly enough for the whole floor to hear.
Hundreds protested the closure outside the district office.
"I'm not even on the schedule today," he protested.
The union protested against the new shift pattern in writing.
She protested that she had been given no warning, and the file showed she was right.

entries.type: reporting verb — a claim the writer strongly doubts
entries.patterns: purport + to-infinitive (the main frame) / purport + that-clause (rare, formal)
entries.never: purport someone to do something; purport + -ing; purport + noun phrase
entries.meaning: What a thing presents itself as being, with the writer's clear suggestion that it may be nothing of the kind. It is the sharpest doubt marker available for documents and objects: a memo purporting to show the transfer tells the reader the memo may well be a forgery. Human subjects are possible but the verb reaches full force with inanimate ones.
entries.transform: "This recording is from the night of the fire." -> A recording purporting to be from the night of the fire was entered into evidence.
examples: The site posted a document purporting to be an internal audit.
She produced a letter purporting to authorize the withdrawal.
The study purports to measure attention span, but it measures reaction time.
His purported resignation was never signed.
The caller purportedly worked for the county assessor's office.
Nothing in the archive purports to be a complete record.

entries.type: reporting verb — a commitment restated on the record
entries.patterns: reaffirm + that-clause / reaffirm + noun phrase / reaffirm + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: reaffirm someone that; reaffirm to do something
entries.meaning: Stating again, formally, a position already taken — the re- does real work, because the verb presupposes the earlier statement. Use it only where the reader knows what is being restated. Compare reiterate, which carries impatience, and confirm, which answers a question rather than restating a promise.
entries.transform: "Our commitment to the alliance has not changed," she said. -> She reaffirmed that their commitment to the alliance had not changed.
examples: The board reaffirmed its commitment to the scholarship fund.
She reaffirmed that no data had left the building.
The court reaffirmed a rule it had announced twenty years earlier.
Both governments reaffirmed the borders set out in the 1997 treaty.
He reaffirmed the timeline without offering any new evidence for it.
Nothing in the statement reaffirmed the original spending figure.

entries.type: reporting verb — a statement repeated, usually because it was ignored
entries.patterns: reiterate + that-clause / reiterate + noun phrase / reiterate + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: reiterate someone that; reiterate to do something; and avoid the redundant reiterate again
entries.meaning: Saying again what has already been said, with a distinct note of impatience — the verb implies the first time did not take. It presupposes the earlier statement, like reaffirm, but where reaffirm is ceremonial and forward-looking, reiterate is corrective.
entries.transform: "As I said before, the account was closed in April," he said. -> He reiterated that the account had been closed in April.
examples: She reiterated that the offer would expire at midnight.
He reiterated the same three objections he had raised in June.
The chair reiterated to the room that questions would come at the end.
I'll reiterate it one last time so nobody can claim they weren't told.
The letter reiterates a demand the company has already refused twice.
Nothing was gained by reiterating a position everyone had already rejected.

entries.type: reporting verb — a condition laid down, or a fact agreed to
entries.patterns: stipulate + that-clause (bare subjunctive in the requirement sense, indicative in the agreement sense) / stipulate + noun phrase / stipulate + to + noun phrase (American legal: agree a fact need not be proved) / stipulate + for + noun phrase
entries.never: stipulate someone to do something; stipulate someone that
entries.meaning: Two related acts. In contracts, setting out a term that binds someone — and there the that-clause takes the bare subjunctive, exactly as after insist and demand: the lease stipulates that the deposit be paid before move-in. In American courtrooms, agreeing that a fact need not be proved, and there the clause is an ordinary indicative one that backshifts: the parties stipulated that the signature was genuine.
entries.transform: "The deposit must be paid before move-in," the lease says. -> The lease stipulates that the deposit be paid before move-in.
examples: The grant stipulates that the funds be spent within eighteen months.
Her father's will stipulated a trust for each grandchild.
The defense stipulated that the video was authentic.
The agreement stipulates that neither side discuss the terms publicly.
He stipulated only one condition: that his name stay off the building.
Nothing in the policy stipulates a maximum number of claims per year.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.register: neutral; very common in news writing
entries.patterns: stress + that-clause / stress + noun phrase / stress + wh-clause / stress + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: stress someone that; stress to do something; stress on
entries.meaning: The same act as emphasize, one syllable shorter, and for that reason the newsroom default. It is factive — he stressed that the vote was nonbinding commits the writer to the vote being nonbinding — and it implies no resistance, which is what separates it from insist.
entries.transform: "And I want to be clear about this: nothing has been decided," she said. -> She stressed that nothing had been decided.
examples: The spokesman stressed that the recall covered only one production run.
She stressed how quickly the situation could change.
He stressed the importance of getting the paperwork in early.
The doctor stressed to both parents that the fever was not dangerous.
Every version of the memo stressed confidentiality.
She stressed that she was speaking for herself and not for the department.

entries.type: reporting verb — a proposition advanced deferentially
entries.patterns: submit + that-clause / submit + to sb + that-clause / submit + noun phrase (put forward for consideration; also hand in) / submit + to + noun phrase (yield to)
entries.never: submit someone that; submit to do something in the assertion sense
entries.meaning: Putting a proposition to somebody who has the authority to reject it. I submit that... is a hedge and a challenge at once: it defers in form while asserting in substance, which is why it belongs to advocates addressing a judge and scholars addressing a field. Outside those settings it sounds stiff.
entries.transform: "In our view, the clause has never applied here," counsel said. -> Counsel submitted that the clause had never applied.
examples: Counsel submits that the evidence was obtained without a warrant.
I submit that we have been solving the wrong problem for two years.
She submitted that the earlier reading of the statute could not survive.
He submitted, with respect, that the committee had exceeded its authority.
It is submitted that no other reading of the clause is available.
The paper submits a simpler explanation than the one currently accepted.

entries.type: reporting verb — a statement or promise made under oath, or with maximum personal warranty
entries.patterns: swear + that-clause / swear + to-infinitive / swear + to sb + that-clause / swear + sb + to + noun phrase / swear + sb + in (install by oath) / swear + to + noun phrase / swear + on + noun phrase / swear + at sb (curse)
entries.never: swear someone that; swear someone to do something meaning promise them
entries.meaning: Asserting with the strongest personal guarantee available, either formally under oath or informally as an emphatic denial (I swear I didn't touch it). In legal settings the alternative is affirm, for witnesses who decline an oath. The curse sense, swear at someone, is a separate verb sharing the form. Irregular: swear, swore, sworn.
entries.transform: "I did not see the car at all," she said. -> She swore that she had not seen the car.
examples: He swore that the safe had been locked when he left.
She swore to tell the truth and then said almost nothing for an hour.
They swore us to secrecy before showing us the prototype.
I swear I put the keys on the hook.
He was sworn in as a judge on a Tuesday afternoon.
She'd swear to it in court if anyone asked her.

entries.type: reporting verb — sworn statement given in a proceeding
entries.patterns: testify + that-clause / testify + to + noun phrase or -ing / testify + about/against/for + noun phrase / testify + before + noun phrase
entries.never: testify someone that; testify to do something; testify to + that-clause
entries.meaning: Giving evidence on the record, under oath, in a court or a hearing. The verb carries no stance of its own — it neither endorses nor doubts, because its whole point is the forum: what matters is that the statement was made where perjury is a crime. An inanimate subject shifts the sense toward attest.
entries.transform: "I was in the parking lot at the time," she said on the stand. -> She testified that she had been in the parking lot at the time.
examples: Three former employees testified that the logs had been altered.
She testified before the subcommittee for nearly five hours.
He refused to testify against his own brother.
The expert testified to the reliability of the test.
She was subpoenaed but never actually testified.
Nothing he testified to at trial matched his earlier statement to police.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.register: neutral, but British-leaning; American writing prefers underscore
entries.patterns: underline + that-clause / underline + noun phrase / underline + wh-clause / underline + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: underline someone that; underline to do something
entries.meaning: Drawing attention to something already said, exactly as emphasize does, by the metaphor of a pen under a line of text. Both underline and underscore are current in American English, but American editors reach for underscore by a wide margin in the figurative sense. Factive, like the rest of the emphasis group.
entries.transform: "And note that this is a one-time payment," she said. -> She underlined that the payment was a one-time one.
examples: She underlined that the arrangement was temporary.
The delay underlines how fragile the supply chain still is.
He underlined the words no exceptions twice in red ink.
Her resignation underlined the depth of the disagreement.
The report underlines a problem the board has known about for years.
Nothing in his answer underlined the urgency the memo had described.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.register: neutral, journalistic; the standard American choice
entries.patterns: underscore + that-clause / underscore + noun phrase / underscore + wh-clause / underscore + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: underscore someone that; underscore to do something
entries.meaning: The American twin of underline and the more idiomatic of the two in figurative use. It works with a speaker but is especially at home with an inanimate subject, where an event rather than a person does the emphasizing: the outage underscored how little redundancy the system had. Factive.
entries.transform: "This is exactly the kind of failure we warned about," she said. -> She underscored that it was the kind of failure they had warned about.
examples: She underscored that the vote was advisory and nothing more.
The outage underscored how little redundancy the network had.
He underscored the importance of documenting every change.
The two resignations underscore a problem the board has ignored.
Her opening remarks underscored what the written report only implied.
Nothing in the briefing underscored the cost, which is what everyone wanted to hear about.

entries.type: reporting verb — a solemn personal promise
entries.patterns: vow + to-infinitive / vow + that-clause / vow + to sb + that-clause / vow + noun phrase
entries.never: vow someone to do something; vow someone that
entries.meaning: A promise made with personal solemnity and, usually, some defiance. It is the headline writer's verb of choice because it is short and dramatic, and it differs from pledge in being personal rather than institutional and from swear in requiring no oath. Do not confuse it with avow, which is an admission, not a promise.
entries.transform: "I will fight this to the last court there is," he said. -> He vowed to fight it to the last court there was.
examples: She vowed to appeal the ruling within the week.
He vowed that no one would be evicted while he was in office.
The company vowed revenge in the trade press and then quietly settled.
They exchanged vows in front of about forty people.
He vowed never to set foot in the building again.
Nobody who vowed to read the whole report actually did.
